title: Pingline Coldwave bench journal - probing burst-coldstart interaction
content:
Context and motivation:
- Trying a new arrival pattern I call 'pingline': repeated short high-frequency ping bursts (20-60 reqs in 200-800ms windows) separated by quiet gaps (~10-30s). Rationale: simulates interactive chat + background polling from mobile clients.
- Observed problem class: when idle gaps expire small per-host KV cache/priming TTLs, the first few bursts see heavy cold-path overhead (recompiles, kernel wakeups, KV miss prefill). Results in p99 spikes (x4-6) and visible tail amplification across replicas.

Experiment summary (configs):
- Model binary: open-llama-7B-compat (quantized). Sequence length: 512 tokens average.
- Fleet: 4 x A100 equivalent instances; 2 worker threads per GPU (continuous-batching enabled).
- Arrival shapes: pingline-short (30 reqs, 400ms), pingline-long (60 reqs, 700ms); quiet gap 20s default.
- Baselines:
  * base: default TTL=12s, no prefill, batch_max=16, batch_timeout=12ms
  * hold-ttl: TTL extended to 60s (cache retention)
content_continued:
* micro-prefill: minimal synthetic prefill (1 small token request) 2s before expected burst
  * adaptive-batch: batch_timeout lowered to 6ms during burst detection window

Raw observations (key runs):
- base (pingline-short): QPS avg 75 during burst, p50=18ms, p95=86ms, p99=310ms, 1.8% errors (timeout retried).
- hold-ttl (pingline-short): p50=20ms, p95=90ms, p99=120ms (down 61% vs base), errors 0.3%. Memory pressure up by ~6% (KV entries retained).
- micro-prefill (pingline-short): p99=140ms, p95=95ms, p50=22ms. Slightly worse than TTL hold but lowers memory tradeoff.
- adaptive-batch + micro-prefill: p99=110ms, p95=88ms, p50=17ms — seems synergistic.

Pingline-long (60 reqs burst) trends:
- base: p99 frequently >600ms, increased queuing and some worker thread stalls observed (GC/kernels).
- hold-ttl: p99 ~180ms, sustained throughput but higher GPU utilization (8-12% higher).

Notes on instrumentation and what I looked at:
- Trace snippets showed first few requests in each burst had a ~60-120ms extra gap spent in KV repopulate (disk->mem cache + LRU churn).
- Kernel/wakeup cost: some worker threads went through cold path compile/kernels which added ~30-50ms per first-token.
- Observed inter-replica amplification: when one replica hit cold path, request routing retried to other replicas causing cascade. Need to verify fallback critical sections.

Quick ASCII latency profile (sample run, base, pingline-short):
- p50 |==== (18ms)
- p95 |================ (86ms)
- p99 |======================================== (310ms)

Interim hypotheses and takeaways:
1) Short TTLs (12s) + occasional idle gaps creates repeatedly cold-baked costs that dominate tail for these real-world mobile patterns.
2) Extending TTL is the most blunt but effective lever for reducing tail; it's a memory vs tail tradeoff. For typical customers this may be acceptable if memory overhead is monitored.
3) Micro-prefill (cheap synthetic requests) is promising: gets most of the tail reduction at much lower memory cost but requires an accurate predictor for when bursts occur (or a cheap periodic keepalive).
4) Adaptive batching helps when bursts are dense: reduces queuing jitter and keeps GPU kernels hot.
5) Routing/fallback logic currently amplifies coldness; need safer fallbacks (circuit-breaker style) to avoid cascade.

Quick checklist (next experiments):
- [ ] Run TTL grid: 8s / 20s / 60s / 120s and measure p99 vs memory.
- [ ] Evaluate prefill schedule: periodic (every 15s) vs predictive (based on client heartbeat) vs reactive (on low-latency probe).
- [ ] Add small-buffered warm lane: keep 2 warm containers per shard reserved for short bursts, compare cost.
- [ ] Measure impact on multi-tenant noisy neighbors when we hold TTL longer.
- [ ] Re-run with real client mixes (50% short, 50% long seq) and observe if TTL still wins.

Commands and notes to reproduce (for my future self):
- bench script: ./tools/bench --pattern pingline --burst-size 30 --burst-width 400 --gap 20 --qps 80 --model open-llama-7b-q
- capture traces: TRACE=1 ./tools/bench ... ; traces written to /tmp/traces/pingline-<ts>.json
- useful debug flags: RUNTIME_KV_TTL=12/60, BATCH_TIMEOUT_MS=12/6, PREFILL=on

Loose notes / thoughts:
- Could try a TTL decay curve depending on observed usage frequency: short TTL for low-usage tenants, longer for tenants with intermittent pingline patterns.
- Consider adding a low-cost heartbeat API for mobile SDKs to inform the control plane of expected bursts (privacy/opt-in).
- Evaluate whether we can compress KV entries to reduce memory overhead for longer TTL.

Summary for now (one-liner):
- For pingline-style arrival with 20s+ gaps, holding per-host state (TTL ~60s) or a cheap micro-prefill combined with adaptive batching reduces p99 by ~50-80% with acceptable resource tradeoffs.

Open questions I want to bring to the team meeting:
- Is increasing default TTL for hosted tenants acceptable given memory budgets? (SRE + infra tradeoff)
- Can adaptive prefill be implemented in the control plane without exponential blast to GPUs?
- Should routing fallback be modified to avoid cross-replica amplification during cold paths?

References and pointers inside repo:
- runtime perf PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/782
- ticket tracking: JIRA PERF-3245 (ColdWave/pingline)

End of notebook entry.
